Refuse: Centred headline over centred subhead over two centred buttons, full-viewport height
Instead: Pick the hero from the page's job: a product needs the product visible, a service needs proof, an editorial page needs a first paragraph. Off-centre is allowed and usually better
Why: It is the shape every model reaches for first, so a visitor has seen it a hundred times this month. Recognisable as machine-made before a word is read

Refuse: Three equal cards in a row, each an icon over a bold noun over two lines of grey text
Instead: Vary the count and weight — two cards where one matters more, four where they are peers, or a list where cards add nothing. Let one item be larger if it is more important
Why: Three equal cards say every feature matters equally, which is never true, and the shape carries no information

Refuse: #6366F1 to #8B5CF6 or any indigo-violet gradient as the default brand colour
Instead: Derive from the site's own brand. Where nothing exists, take the palette from the trade, not from fashion
Why: It is the default of the tools, not of the site. A tour operator and a dentist end up identical

Refuse: Every section on the same vertical padding, so the page reads as a stack of equal boxes
Instead: Vary the rhythm — tighter where content is dense, generous around the one thing that matters. Rhythm is how a page shows what it thinks is important
Why: Equal spacing flattens hierarchy. The eye is given no reason to stop anywhere

Refuse: Paragraphs running the full width of a wide container
Instead: 60-75 characters per line. Constrain the text, not the section
Why: Long measures are measurably harder to read, and nothing says unconsidered faster than a 200-character line

Refuse: font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem) or any viewport-scaled type
Instead: Use the site's own text tokens — ACSS var(--text-l
Why: 20px) with a px or em fallback
column7: House rule. Fluid type fights the design system the site already has and produces sizes nobody chose

Refuse: An icon above every heading, chosen for decoration rather than meaning
Instead: Use icons where they carry meaning — a payment method, a file type, a platform. Otherwise leave them out
Why: Decorative icons add visual noise and no information, and generic icon sets are instantly recognisable

Refuse: Grey boxes or stock-shaped placeholders used as structural elements
Instead: Design for the images the site actually has. Where there are none, use type, colour and space to carry the layout
Why: A layout that only works once someone finds photographs is a layout that does not work

Refuse: Centre alignment on headings, body, buttons and cards throughout
Instead: Left-align body text by default. Centre short things only — a single heading, a small call to action
Why: Centred body text has ragged left edges that slow reading, and total symmetry reads as a template

Refuse: A drop shadow on every card, button, input and section
Instead: Pick one elevation language and use it sparingly. Most surfaces need a border or a background shift, not a shadow
Why: Shadows everywhere means depth nowhere. It is the fastest way to make a page look like a component demo

Refuse: Three invented testimonials with placeholder avatars and five stars
Instead: Use real proof or none. One genuine quote beats three invented ones, and no proof beats fake proof
Why: Fabricated social proof is a lie on the client's website, and readers recognise the shape

Refuse: Fast. Secure. Reliable. Scalable. — single-word claims with no object
Instead: Say what it does for whom. A claim with a subject and an object is worth ten adjectives
Why: Adjective lists are filler that survives because they are easy to generate, not because they persuade

Refuse: Emoji standing in for interface or feature icons
Instead: Use the site's icon set, or type. Emoji render differently on every platform and cannot be styled
Why: It reads as a draft, and on a client's site it reads as carelessness

Refuse: background-clip: text gradients on headings
Instead: Solid colour from the palette. Weight and size carry emphasis
Why: Low contrast in practice, unreliable across browsers, and dated the moment it was everywhere

Refuse: Every section fading and sliding in as it enters the viewport
Instead: Motion on one or two deliberate moments, respecting prefers-reduced-motion
Why: Universal scroll animation delays every read and makes a page feel slower than it is

Refuse: A dark theme made by flipping black and white
Instead: Build the dark palette properly — surfaces lighten with elevation, not by inverting, and colours need adjusting to hold contrast
Why: Inverted palettes produce muddy greys and unreadable brand colours

Refuse: Invented UI screenshots showing charts of nothing
Instead: Show the real product, or describe it in words. An abstract shape is more honest than a fabricated screen
Why: A fabricated screenshot is a claim about a product that does not look like that

Refuse: Get Started next to Learn More, every time
Instead: One primary action that names what happens. A secondary only where a genuine second path exists
Why: Two generic buttons split attention and neither says where it goes

Rule: Section headings that name the section
Refuse: Our Features. Our Services. Testimonials. FAQ.
Instead: Headings that carry the actual claim — what the features do, who the service is for
Why: A label tells the reader nothing they could not see. It is a wasted line at the top of every section

Refuse: Forcing equal-height cards by truncating content with ellipses
Instead: Let content set the height, or edit the content until it fits honestly
Why: Truncation hides the thing the card exists to say
